Garrett is plenty good and maybe on his way to becoming even great. But if he truly wants to establish himself within the elite tier, he will have to achieve an Aaron Donald-type status and become equally as dominant when defending the run. Garrett’s three-year run-defense grade of 80.2 ranks only 13th among 96 edge players who played at least 300 run-defense snaps from 2017 to 2019. His 4.3% run-stop percentage ranks only 44th.
With time on his side, Garrett has all the tools to quickly develop into one of the game’s best players at his position. However, he must learn to play with a better temperament and avoid costly penalties and uncontrollable outbursts. Unfortunately, his past trouble will create a small margin for similar behavior moving forward, but given the nature of his true character when he entered the league, Garrett is almost certainly a sure thing to deliver a return on investment upon his return.

title: ‘TUF’ champ James Wilks finds second life — and controversy — as plant-based-diet advocate
website_text:
Becoming a magnet for controversy has been a strange experience for James Wilks.
The mostly mild-mannered former winner of the UFC’s “The Ultimate Fighter” reality show knew co-producing and starring in a documentary about his journey from mixed martial artist to staunch vegan would be unpopular in some circles. Still, since his documentary “The Game Changers,” has become a modest hit on streaming services after its 2018 release, Wilks (7-4) sounded a bit bemused by some of the reaction.
Advertisement
“The vast majority of the response that we’ve been getting through ‘Game Changers’ or through my personal Instagram page has been overwhelmingly positive,” Wilks said. “Now, of course, we’re getting pushback from a number of sectors. … I mean, you’ve got to take the bad with the good, (but) I have people messaging me talking mad crap or even people talking about my wife or my kids. I get everything that goes with it.”
Wilks has clashed with Piers Morgan during a TV appearance and sparred with author and diet guru Chris Kresser in a nearly four-hour-long debate on Joe Rogan’s mega-popular podcast. Googling the documentary, which unapologetically challenges much of the conventional wisdom about how people eat, brings up no shortage of YouTube videos with titles like “Scientist Fact-Checks the Game Changers Documentary” and “Game Changers DEBUNKED!”
All the attention — positive and negative — is something Wilks said he’s gotten more comfortable with over time, but he insisted becoming a de facto public face of plant-based diets wasn’t his original plan.
“I didn’t want to be in the film,” he said. “If you look at the early pitch tapes when we were trying to tell people what we were doing, I wasn’t even in it. I sort of begrudgingly said yes originally, but now I feel like I’m getting more suited to the role.”
“The Game Changers” has spent time on both Netflix and Amazon Prime since its release, has a 99 percent audience rating on Rotten Tomatoes (along with a 70 percent overall mark from critics), an 8.0 rating on IMDB and boasts a bevy of star-studded supporters such as executive producers James Cameron, Jackie Chan, Pamela Anderson and Arnold Schwarzenegger.
Schwarzenegger also appears in the film, talking about his own transition from meat-loving bodybuilder to 72-year-old who eats mostly plants. Pro athletes such as NFL players Derrick Morgan and Griff Whalen, Olympic cyclist Dotsie Bausch, weightlifter Kendrick Farris, boxer Bryant Jennings and strongman Patrik Baboumian all appear as well, evangelizing the vegan lifestyle.
The final version of the documentary is as slick and entertaining as any Hollywood blockbuster.
Back in 2011, however, it was just Wilks, looking for answers as his fighting career ended on the heels of a series of injuries.
Advertisement
Most MMA fans remember Wilks, now 41 and a native of Leicestershire, England, as the surprise winner of “The Ultimate Fighter: United States vs. United Kingdom” in 2009. But after hoisting the TUF trophy, he went on to have just four fights in the UFC octagon — putting up a 2-2 record — before retiring in 2012 at age 34.
Wilks, a welterweight, said he suffered torn ligaments in both knees while training with future heavyweight champion Fabricio Werdum for a short-notice bout in 2011. While working his way back from those setbacks, he also aggravated a years-old neck injury. The ensuing MRI revealed stenosis, a narrowing of the passageways within the neck, which can put pressure on the nerves or spinal cord.
“I went to multiple specialists, and they all said I had a significantly high risk of paralysis (if I kept fighting),” Wilks said. “So, at that point, I just didn’t think it was really worth it, and I made the decision to medically retire.”
While laid up from the injuries, Wilks said he began researching different kinds of nutrition for optimal physical recovery and athletic performance. He soon began to encounter information about the benefits of plant-based diets. He said he was skeptical at first, thinking a vegan or vegetarian approach might work for a runner or tennis player, but not for an athlete primarily interested in a strength and endurance sport like fighting.
Then Wilks said he happened upon a study — one later debated by critics after the release of “The Game Changer” — showing that many Roman gladiators may have consumed a predominantly vegetarian diet. As a combat sports enthusiast himself, Wilks said locating this study was his “inciting incident,” and he decided to give going meat-free a try.
Over a short period of time, he transitioned away from meat and dairy — first cutting out red meat, then chicken, fish and ultimately all animal products entirely. The effects on his body and overall health, he said, were immediate. In another scene recreated for “The Game Changers,” Wilks said six weeks into his new vegan diet he went to his California-based MMA gym and set a new house record with an hour-long workout on the battle ropes.
After that, there was no going back.
Advertisement
“My endurance went way up,” he said. “Another thing that I didn’t talk about in the film was, my strength went up also.”
Wilks said the more he learned and experienced about plant-based diets, the more he understood that much of what he’d believed about consuming meat and protein just wasn’t true. He was breaking through performance plateaus in the MMA gym and the weight room, some of which he said had dogged him for years. Finally, Wilks said he decided he’d been misled by society’s attitudes toward “healthy” diets and perhaps by the meat and dairy industry itself.
Not long after, he said he woke up in the middle of the night with a sudden realization: He needed to spread the word.
“I literally woke up at 2 o’clock in the morning and thought, ‘I’ve got to tell everybody about this. I’ve got to make a documentary,’” Wilks said.
There was just one problem: He didn’t know the first thing about how to do that.
Wilks didn’t have much money. He didn’t have any equipment. He didn’t know anybody in the film industry. He didn’t even really know anyone in the plant-based diet space. But he called-up the one contact he did have, a former director of photography on “The Ultimate Fighter,” and asked for pointers on equipment and technique.
“I went on Craigslist and bought a used camera,” he said. “Then I went onto YouTube and did a three-point lighting (tutorial). I bought some wireless mics. Then, I started looking around at people I could interview.”
Wilks said he was surprised at first how many top-level athletes he found who were already eating plant-based diets. At first, he had no travel budget, so he mostly had to stick to talking to athletes in the Los Angeles area. But he started shooting, sometimes even just using his phone, though he admitted not much of his earliest footage made it into the movie’s final version.
Advertisement
In time, he met co-producer Joseph Pace, and the two of them began collaborating. By 2013 they’d taken on another producer and started exploratory filming in a more professional way than Wilks could muster on his own. Things really got serious in 2014, he said, when the team hired award-winning documentary director Louie Psihoyos and eventually won the support of blockbuster director and producer Cameron. By 2015 production on what would eventually become “The Game Changers” was underway.
The finished product is undeniably eye-opening. If there’s one problem with “The Game Changers” it’s that perhaps it’s a little bit too persuasive. The movie advocates for plant-based diets and indicts the meat industry on so many fronts, it’s understandable that skeptics might come away unsure if everything in it could really be true.
Among other things, “The Game Changers” provides evidence that a plant-based diet improves general health and wellness, weight loss, cholesterol, blood flow and sexual prowess. It charges the meat industry with whitewashing the harmful health effects of meat-heavy diets, just as tobacco companies did with cigarette smoking for much of the 20th century. It also highlights the industry’s negative effects on the environment and — without ever coming right out and using the phrase — on climate change.
The documentary even takes time to spotlight the first fight between Nate Diaz and Conor McGregor at UFC 196 in 2016. During the lead-up to that big-money welterweight bout, McGregor talked about how much meat he was eating during training, in an effort to bulk up to 170-pounds. Meanwhile, Diaz is known as one of MMA’s highest-profile vegans. On fight night, McGregor started strong but faded in the second round, ultimately losing to Diaz via rear-naked choke.
Leading up to the pair’s second fight at UFC 202 later that year, which McGregor won, the Irishman said he’d changed his diet, among other things, to correct the mistakes of the first bout.
Wilks conceded he didn’t know how much McGregor’s change in diet had to do with the different outcomes — the second fight didn’t make the cut into the documentary’s final version — but also said it probably wasn’t a complete non-factor, either.
“I think even in Conor’s own words, he felt like (the first fight) was a battle of energy,” he said. “Sure, there was a weight difference, but he was trying to basically put on a bunch of weight by eating a bunch of steak. We just know in terms of endurance and blood flow, that is not going to be helpful.”
Advertisement
Not everybody has bought into every claim in the film. Critics have picked at “The Game Changers” for presenting an incomplete picture during its one hour, 48-minute runtime and for its occasionally hokey dramatizations of scientific experiments. But Wilks said he stands behind everything in the movie.
Moving forward, he said he’ll continue to advocate for people eating less meat and more plants. He said “The Game Changers” website is a good resource for people who are interested in finding out more, that he’ll soon be putting out a book under the brand and that the team there will also release more footage from the documentary.
Wilks said he isn’t a zealot. He doesn’t insist everyone go vegan or vegetarian or anything else. But he said he believes the evidence is clear on the effects of plant-based diets, both for average citizens and professional athletes.
“It doesn’t have to be all or nothing,” Wilks said. “Studies show that any push toward getting more whole plant foods in your diet shows health benefits and it’s very likely that the same biological mechanisms that impact health also impact performance.”
(Top photo: Denise Truscello / WireImage)

title: Syracuse pulls Kiss Cam after forced, on-screen kiss sparks controversy
website_text:
Syracuse pulls Kiss Cam after forced, on-screen kiss sparks controversy
Syracuse University is considering kissing its Kiss Cam goodbye after a fan suggested it sends the wrong message at a time when colleges are fighting against campus sexual violence.
A regular feature at sports venues, the Kiss Cam frames unsuspecting couples in a heart on the Jumbotron while the game crowd cheers for them to kiss. Hearts melted when cancer-stricken former President Jimmy Carter and wife Rosalynn obliged during an Atlanta Braves game last week.
But Steve Port of Manlius said what he saw during the Sept. 12 football game between Syracuse University and Wake Forest constituted unacceptable behavior, and maybe even assault, as men forcibly kissed women who were clearly saying no.
In one of two examples, he said a woman's head shake was met with "no less than six sets of hands from the seats around her shov(ing) her unwilling face into his." The crowd cheered, he wrote in a letter to the editor, which generated hundreds of comments on Syracuse.com, both agreeing and disagreeing with him.
"Honestly, I wasn't out to kill the Kiss Cam," Port said by phone Tuesday. "I was just out to raise an important issue that I saw happening and that's important to me. I've always kind of been a little put off by it anyway, but never witnessed an actual act of -- oh, my God, this woman is saying no and it didn't matter."
The kiss cam feature was pulled from Saturday's game against Central Michigan University, Sue Edson, a Syracuse University athletics spokeswoman, said.
"We are taking the time to assess the concerns expressed in the letter to the editor," she said.
Syracuse University senior Elaina Crockett suggested the university poll students on whether to keep the feature or come up with some Kiss Cam rules, including moving on quickly if someone obviously doesn't want to play along.
Crockett, who writes a column about gender and sexuality for The Daily Orange student newspaper, said that otherwise it's counter to today's emphasis on affirmative consent that stresses communication and respect for boundaries as a way to reduce campus sexual assaults.
"Just because I'm sitting somewhere doesn't mean that I'm entitled to kiss this stranger. That's a horrible assumption that we've created," she said by phone.
The university isn't the only venue rethinking its kiss cam. The New York Mets last week apologized and said they would stop showing two opposing players inside the heart as a joke after some fans complained it was offensive to gay people.
"While intended to be lighthearted, we unintentionally offended some," the Mets said in a statement. "Our organization is wholly supportive of fostering an inclusive and respectful environment at games."

title: Logan Paul and NFL Player Antonio Brown Spark Boxing Fight Rumors
website_text:
- Logan Paul, the controversial YouTube star, has been exploring an interest in professional boxing, and recently fought — and lost — a fight against fellow YouTuber KSI.
- Paul's next boxing opponent may be NFL player Antonio Brown. The two exchanged insults on Twitter late Monday night, hinting that they would "square up" and fight sometime in the future.
- Both Paul and Brown have left paths of controversy in their careers: Paul has made YouTube videos showing a dead body and tasing dead rats, and Brown was recently accused to rape and is currently struggling to find a team to sign him.
- Visit Business Insider's homepage for more stories.
YouTube personality Logan Paul may have only fought one other YouTuber so far in his pursuit of a professional boxing career, but it appears he's looking to raise the stakes by possibly taking on controversial football player Antonio Brown.
Although no punches have yet to be thrown, Paul and Brown traded figurative jabs late Monday night on Twitter. After Brown tweeted at Paul to "square up," Paul responded an hour later with a comeback about Brown's short stint with the NFL team the New England Patriots, who dropped him from their roster after just 13 days.
"I'd drop you faster than the patriots," Paul tweeted back at Brown. The Twitter fight comes a week after Paul appeared on Barstool Sports' KFC Radio, where he called out Brown by name and said he wanted to "f--k (him) up."
—Logan Paul (@LoganPaul) January 7, 2020
Rumors about the fight have already gained traction across the internet, which was just recently treated to rumors that Paul had appeared in a (likely fake) sex tape. Sports-betting platform Odds Shark has even released opening odds for a "potential match" between the two, which favor Paul to win.
Representatives for Brown and Paul did not respond to requests for comment.
In a high-profile celebrity boxing match in November, Paul fought fellow YouTuber KSI and lost. Paul, 24, recently told Business Insider about his plans to pursue a career as a professional boxer outside of creating YouTube videos. Despite his minimal experience and losing record, Paul has said he wants to fight again, and has challenged Conor McGregor to a fight on at least two separate occasions.
Meanwhile, Brown finds himself without a job amid the NFL post-season playoffs. Brown, a celebrated receiver, saw his status in the NFL dwindle in 2019. Brown has been a free agent since September, when the New England Patriots released him just 13 days after signing a one-year deal. In those 13 days, reports emerged accusing Brown of raping his former fitness trainer and sending "intimidating" messages to a second accuser.
Just this week, Brown dropped an auto-tuned rap song and an accompanying music video, which has been met with negative feedback online.
Paul has also faced controversies and career setbacks in recent years. After staying scandal-free for the start of his career, Paul has made a series of missteps. In 2017, Paul released a video showing a dead body in Japan's "suicide forest," a highly criticized incident that negatively impacted his fanbase and led many to question his judgment. He followed the scandal with a video showing him tasing dead rats, and has also made racist and homophobic remarks on Twitter and his podcast.
When Forbes released its list of the highest-paid YouTubers at the end of 2019, Paul and his brother, Jake, both failed to place on the list.

title: Brent Musburger still thinks Katherine Webb controversy was silly
website_text:
Brent Musburger still thinks Katherine Webb controversy was silly
Brent Musburger famously called Katherine Webb (now Katherine McCarron) "lovely" and a "beautiful woman" during a national title game four-and-a-half years ago.
Some people were offended by the remarks, and the now-retired broadcast legend still to this day gets asked about the fallout from his comments on A.J. McCarron's significant other.
Musburger was recently asked about the controversy during an interview with SECCountry.com. The former ESPN legend feels the same way today as he did in 2013, saying, "I called a beauty queen beautiful. Give me a break. I mean, come on. That was like, ’What are you talking about?'"
In addition to the remarks on Webb's looks, Musburger also said to his broadcast partner, Kirk Herbsteit, “You quarterbacks get all the good-looking women.”
In the interview with SECCountry.com, Musburger said that comment was meant for Herbstreit, a former Ohio State quarterback.
"I had just been out to dinner with Herbstreit and his wife the night before. So the rest of the comments were addressed to him. … I thought it was silly, to tell you the truth.”
As for today, Musburger had more of the same to say. “I wish them the best," he said. "And AJ, I'm glad that they're happily married. I hope they live happily ever after. … Katherine remains beautiful, in my opinion.”

title: Killer bees, Simpsons controversy & more: Louisiana sports in pop culture guide
website_text:
It’s not out of the ordinary to hear LSU and the Saints mentioned in popular culture lately, thanks to their recent successes, but that certainly hasn’t always been the case. Spotting obscure references has been a fun game, especially when they’re unexpected.
Why was an extra in an early ’90s episode of “Saved by the Bell” wearing an LSU hat? Wasn’t it weird that Ted Mosby of “How I Met Your Mother” was spotted wearing a Saints shirt, even though he was born and raised in Ohio?
Advertisement
It’s fun to spot nods to Louisiana sports, from the “blink and you’ll miss it” references to the obvious, such as cameos from Saints players and coaches on “Ballers.” Commercials aren’t referenced here, although there have been a few of those from Drew Brees and also former Saints quarterback Luke McCown, who starred in a national Verizon commercial a few years back.
I also didn’t include instances in “Treme” and “NCIS: New Orleans,” which have too many to mention due to their setting. There were also some TV shows that had characters who went to Louisiana schools without it being a major plot point (Dr. Dennis Gant in “ER” went to LSU medical school; Dr. Preston Burke in “Grey’s Anatomy” attended Tulane).
I also didn’t include IFC’s “Brockmire,” although Hank Azaria’s character, Jim Brockmire, becomes the play-by-play announcer for the AAA New Orleans Crawdaddy’s in the second season. The New Orleans Baby Cakes actually ran a promo in 2018 where the team wore Crawdaddy’s uniforms for a night. However, the show is about a fictional team, so it didn’t make the cut.
In the movie realm, be sure to check out my colleague Chris Vannini’s breakdown of the fictional SCLSU defender Bobby Boucher’s tackling in “The Waterboy,” written as part of The Athletic’s sports in movies series.
Here are some of the references I gathered from research and some sharp-eyed fans via a social media request. Have something I missed? Send it in via the comment section below.
TV
“The Ellen DeGeneres Show”
Episodes aired:
Multiple
The Saints have been mentioned many times during DeGeneres’ popular talk show, which makes sense considering the host was born in Metairie and went to Grace King High School and UNO. There are probably too many references to name here, but Drew Brees has been a regular guest on her show over the years and DeGeneres had a long segment about the Saints in 2010 after they won the Super Bowl.
Advertisement
“The Super Bowl really was more than just a team winning a game. It gave a city hope that has been through so much. I’m so proud of the Saints and to the city of New Orleans, I’m so, so happy for you,” said DeGeneres, who admitted she’s not much of a football fan.
One notable Saints segment came in 2011 when the Saints “recruited” DeGeneres to their training camp in Oxnard, Calif.
The segment was recently reposted on the show’s official YouTube channel.
“Ballers”
Episode name:
“Crumbs”
Episode aired: Sept. 22. 2019
Saints running back Alvin Kamara makes a cameo in this episode, which revolves around fictional Rams GM Charles Greane trying to sign him even though he is told Kamara isn’t leaving New Orleans. Kamara remarks that the Rams “stole one from them,” referring to the real NFC Championship Game that had occurred a few months prior.
Episode name: “Elidee”
Episode aired: July 31, 2016
Saints coach Sean Payton makes a cameo as himself, trying to recruit fictional wide receiver Ricky Jerret to sign with New Orleans. The episode opens with a plane prominently featuring the Saints logo as a team employee meets Jerret at the airport. Later on, Jerret asks “where’s the love” and the Saints send him off from the airport with a parade and an appearance from Payton.
When asked later about his guest appearance, Payton joked: “Mickey (Loomis) said to me, ‘If we ever show up with an airplane and a parade to sign a 30-year-old receiver. …'”
“Sesame Street”
Episode name:
“Elmozilla”

“Dr. Who”
Episode name:
“The Impossible Astronaut”

Dr. Who is a long-running British television series that airs on BBC, so this reference makes little sense. In the first episode of the sixth series of the show, an LSU helmet can be spotted sitting on top of a bar.

Episode name:
“Rabbit or Duck”

Barney Stinson goes to the Super Bowl at what was then called Sun Life Stadium in Miami. While the Saints and Colts aren’t specifically mentioned, there is a shot of the field with the team logos visible, and there appears to be footage from the actual game, which aired on CBS the night before. Nancy Donovan, a Patriots fan, is talking to Jack Donaghy about how her husband recently left her to move to New Orleans, prompting this exchange.
Nancy: Oh, God. I swore I wasn’t going to cry in front of you. Mark left. Yesterday. He took a job in New Orleans.
Jack: What? What about his roofing company?
Nancy: Apparently, Brad Pitt and Sharon Stone did a crap job rebuilding those Katrina homes. Mark thinks that he can make a fortune down there. But I know the real reason he left. He wants to force me to be the one to ask for the divorce. …
Jack: Have you talked openly about divorce?
Nancy Donovan: Yeah, we talked to Dr. Phil. And then we made a collage in our dream journals. No. You know how it is up here. People don’t talk. They just run off to New Orleans and jump on that B.S. Saints bandwagon. Go Pats.

Awesom-O

George: “You know what’s interesting. The quarterback for the Atlanta Falcons is Bobby Hebert. No “r,” which I find fascinating. You know it’s Herbert, H-e-r-b-e-r-t, Hebert, H-e-b-e-r-t. “Hebert.” It’s a fun name to pronounce. Try and say it. Hebert. Take a shot. All right.”

Released

“Focus,” starring Will Smith and Margot Robbie is a film about con artists that was shot in New Orleans and also features the city (and the Superdome) as a plot point when the two go to Louisiana with a scheme to steal from people during Super Bowl week. If you look closely enough, you’ll see former Saints tight end Ben Watson and his wife Kirsten riding the escalator in front of Smith and Robbie.
“The Blind Side”
Released:
Nov. 20, 2009
“The Blind Side” was based on the life story of Ole Miss tackle Michael Oher, and several NCAA coaches make appearances. Oher was a freshman at Ole Miss in 2005, so a recruiting montage that would’ve taken place in 2004-2005 ends up being an amusing nod to the ever-changing uniforms of college football coaches. Alabama coach Nick Saban (then at LSU) and LSU coach Ed Orgeron (then at Ole Miss) both make appearances. Saban is also seen in his office with framed newspaper prints of LSU’s national championship and bowl game wins.
Advertisement
“Indecent Proposal”
Released:
April 7, 1993
Woody Harrelson’s character David Murphy wears an LSU hat during a few scenes, although it’s not a plot point.
“Everybody’s All-American”
Released:
Nov. 4, 1988
“Everybody’s All-American,” starring Dennis Quaid, told the story of fictional running back Gavin Grey, who played for fictional Louisiana University (at least in the film version). Although LSU wasn’t mentioned by name, the game scenes were filmed before and during halftime of actual LSU games in 1987.
“We were able to shoot all of our college football sequences inside Tiger Stadium with 90,000 LSU fans looking on,” director Taylor Hackford said in “Behind the Scenes with Hollywood Producers: Interviews with 14 Top Film Creators.” Dennis and our players had rehearsed each play like a performance. I had my camera positions all mapped out. So, 10 minutes before the game, when the stands were full, we ran our plays with military precision. Then at halftime, we ran another series of plays during the seven minutes we were allotted. The resulting shots of Dennis Quaid and his LSU teammates winning the 1959 National Championship in front of 90,000 screaming fans was electrifying.
Rumors have long persisted that the movie, and the book it was based on, was about former LSU running back Billy Cannon, but author Frank Deford always denied this. Cannon also rejected requests to consult with the filmmakers and was not a fan of the movie, according to his biography: “Billy Cannon, a Long, Long Run.”
LSU did earn itself another fan, however, as actor John Goodman, who was also in the movie, routinely showed up in the press box to games in the years after the movie. He also met his future wife in New Orleans while filming the movie and moved to Louisiana.
“Cocktail”
Released:
July 29, 1988
Advertisement
Scenes from a 1987 LSU-Georgia game can be seen playing on a TV behind the bar in this Tom Cruise movie.
“The Savage Bees”
Released:
Nov. 22, 1976
This one might take the award for most obscure reference; a Twitter follower alerted me to its presence. This made-for-TV movie was one of the many films about killer bees that came out in the 70s, and this one was set during Mardi Gras.
While I won’t spoil the absurd plot and ending, the Superdome plays a prominent role in the final minutes in regards to how they defeat the bees. I hope I’ve intrigued everyone enough to go look this up.
“Number One”
Released:
Aug. 21, 1969
Charlton Heston stars as Ron Catalan, an aging quarterback for the Saints who is trying to lead them to another championship. The Saints’ real names and uniforms were used, and the football scenes were shot at Tulane Stadium, where the Saints played at the time. Several players were involved with the movie, including quarterback Billy Kilmer and center Joe Wendryhoski.
The Saints had not actually played a game yet when the movie was greenlit. Bruce Dern, who played Richie Fowler, reflected on the movie in his memoir “Things I’ve Said, But Probably Shouldn’t Have.” Members of the cast spent the first eight weeks traveling with the Saints team, including their very first game.
“This fall, the New Orleans Saints are in their first season,” he was told. “We have a script called ‘Number One’ that’s going to star Charlton Heston as an aging quarterback for the Saints. Everybody knows they’re no good. We’re going to travel with the Saints the first eight weeks of the season and you’re going to play his wide receiver whose in his last year and wants to get out. They’ve all been picked up from other teams because they were in the expansion draft.”

Drake filmed the video in New Orleans and there’s multiple prominent shots of the city throughout, including the Superdome. Blink and you might miss an appearance by Kamara, who has a cameo in a quick shot where he’s sitting next to Drake.

Rick Ross is wearing a purple jacket with one of LSU’s old logos and patches that designate the 1958, 2003 and 2007 national championships. Ross also shared a stage with former LSU coach Les Miles while performing at Kansas’ spring game in 2019.
